$comment: Illustrative cost model for the pipeline explorer. Numbers model two designs of the same DAG, not production measurements. The document profile is a public IETF RFC; stages are described at pattern level only.

document.title: RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics (sections 8–15 profile)
document.note: A public IETF standard stands in for an engineering specification: numbered normative clauses (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), cross-references to other standards, and pages that are pure table of contents or boilerplate.

nodes.label: Admission control
nodes.summary: Bound the number of concurrent analyses (runtime-adjustable) and queue the rest. While a request waits or runs, an empty progress frame goes out every 15 seconds so the reverse proxy never sees an idle stream.
nodes.why: A burst of uploads must degrade to waiting, not to timeouts. The proxy's 60-second idle limit is owned by another team; heartbeats work under it instead of negotiating around it.
nodes.guards: End-to-end cancellation: closing the stream cancels the context, every pending task, and the in-flight upstream calls, then frees the slot within milliseconds.

nodes.label: Ingest & convert
nodes.summary: Fetch the file from object storage and convert PDF, DOCX, XLSX or ReqIF to markdown through the ingestion service's streaming RPC. Pages are also rendered to images for the vision path.
nodes.why: Every later stage reads one normalised representation, so format quirks are handled once, here, and never again downstream.
nodes.guards: Conversion streams per-page progress so a 300-page file never looks stalled. A fuzzy word-anchoring pass repairs vision-model hallucinations inside compound words — German is unforgiving.

nodes.label: Content-hash cache
nodes.summary: Hash the file bytes and look up a previous run. A byte-identical re-upload returns the stored result and skips everything below.
nodes.why: Reviewers re-upload the same document constantly — after a rename, after a merge, to 'refresh'. Paying the full pipeline for that was the single most wasteful thing the first version did.
nodes.guards: Keyed on content, never on filename. A one-byte change is a new document.

nodes.label: Classify document
nodes.summary: One cheap call decides what arrived: a requirements spec, a standards catalogue, a component diagram or a reference document. Everything below branches on that answer.
nodes.why: A spec and a norms catalogue need opposite treatment. Guessing wrong wastes every later call, so the decision is made first, once, cheaply.
nodes.guards: Per-customer document conventions are looked up as hints rather than re-inferred; the answer is a closed enum, so a creative model reply cannot route anywhere unexpected.

nodes.label: Page triage
nodes.summary: Mark tables of contents, title, approval and blank pages as skippable, and estimate how many requirements each remaining page holds.
nodes.why: Roughly a third of a typical document is not extractable. Skipping it is the cheapest optimisation in the pipeline. The per-page estimate is what makes the recall guard possible.
nodes.guards: The naive design asked the model page by page; the batched design shows it the whole page list once, which is both cheaper and more consistent.

nodes.label: Summarise reference doc
nodes.summary: Reference documents and norms catalogues are not extracted; they are summarised (one call for small files, map-reduce for large ones) so they can be attached to the project as context.
nodes.why: Not every upload is a spec. This branch is why classification exists.
nodes.guards: Branch not taken for this document — the counters show zero calls.

nodes.label: Extract requirements
nodes.summary: One strong call per extractable page: the page image is the primary input, the markdown the supplementary context. Output is a JSON list of requirements and standalone standards references.
nodes.why: Layout carries meaning — tables, indents, numbered clauses. Text-only extraction lost it; vision-first extraction keeps it. Pages are independent, so they run concurrently.
nodes.guards: Page metadata (drawing refs, page numbers) is fenced with explicit do-not-extract markers so it cannot become a ghost requirement. Dense norm-list pages get a primer hint with its own timeout.

nodes.label: Standards-code scan
nodes.summary: A prefix-agnostic scanner finds every referenced standard (ISO 8601, RFC 5234, …), canonicalises spelling, expands ranges and merges duplicates across pages. A single cheap call filters false positives at the end.
nodes.why: The first version asked the model to list codes page by page: it missed some, invented others and spelled the same code four ways. Deterministic code is exhaustive; the model is asked only the one question it is good at — is this really a standard?
nodes.guards: Canonicalisation happens before the model sees anything, so it cannot re-introduce duplicates. Validated on a 71-page document with 212 codes.

nodes.label: Recall guard + JSON repair
nodes.summary: Compare each page's yield with the triage estimate; pages far below it are retried with a stronger model and an explicit hint. Truncated or malformed JSON is repaired (fences stripped, open structures closed) and only the missing items are re-requested.
nodes.why: Silent under-extraction is the failure nobody notices until a reviewer does. A count-based guard catches it at pipeline time instead of review time.
nodes.guards: Retries are bounded (one per page) and skip pages that were already primed, so the guard cannot double the cost of a document.

nodes.label: Correction hints
nodes.summary: Every reviewer correction on earlier projects is stored as its own retrievable record (predicted → corrected). The nearest ones are retrieved per batch and injected as hints — only when they cover the batch well enough to help.
nodes.why: The first learning loop summarised corrections into rule files with a pair of models; the rules were generic and untraceable. Retrieving individual corrections keeps provenance and fixed 6/10 → 9/10 on the classification corpus.
nodes.guards: Tenant isolation is enforced client-side on every retrieval and verified in tests; a seven-variant ablation chose the injection format.

nodes.label: Enrich requirements
nodes.summary: Category, criticality, owning team and a first feasibility opinion for each requirement — all four fields from one call over a batch of twelve, with category and team names resolved to database ids by fuzzy match.
nodes.why: Four separate per-requirement stages meant four system prompts, four round-trips and four chances to time out per clause. One batched call also sees neighbouring requirements, which makes labels more consistent.
nodes.guards: Reviewer corrections from earlier projects are retrieved and injected as hints behind a coverage gate; a seven-variant ablation chose the format. Unknown ids never reach the database — unresolved labels fall back to a default.

nodes.label: Evidence retrieval
nodes.summary: For each requirement, search past-project evidence and reference documents with several rewritten queries, then rank hits with per-type floors so historical verdicts are never crowded out.
nodes.why: Without retrieval the model answers from general knowledge and sounds confident about things nobody has ever built.
nodes.guards: Searches run concurrently against the vector store; a near-identical past requirement with an explicit verdict short-circuits the next stage entirely.

nodes.label: Feasibility reasoning
nodes.summary: Reason over ten requirements and their evidence per call, citing evidence by label (H1, R2). Requirements with a high-confidence historical match skip the model.
nodes.why: Batching is what makes a citation check affordable on every requirement rather than a sample.
nodes.guards: Evidence labels are opaque handles: the model cannot cite what it was not shown. About a fifth of requirements short-circuit with zero calls.

nodes.label: Citation check + retry
nodes.summary: Every claim's labels are checked against the retrieved set. Unsupported claims are stripped and the batch is retried once with the stripped claims called out. Never twice.
nodes.why: The naive design had no check — verdicts read well and cited history nobody could open.
nodes.guards: A second failure returns a shorter answer rather than a loop. Only the batches that failed the check (about one in ten) pay for a retry.

nodes.label: Finalize
nodes.summary: Rule-based de-duplication across files, one call to synthesise the project goal, one to extract basic document metadata, and aggregation of the standards list.
nodes.why: De-duplication is a set operation and never needed a model. Keeping it deterministic makes output stable between runs.
nodes.guards: Two model calls per document, fixed, regardless of size.

nodes.label: Translate
nodes.summary: Every requirement text into each target language, twenty-five strings per call, with an in-memory cache so repeated phrases translate once.
nodes.why: One string per call made this the slowest stage in the pipeline for a step that adds no intelligence.
nodes.guards: A failed batch retries item by item so one bad string cannot block a document; an explicit model fallback chain handles provider errors.

nodes.label: Stream result
nodes.summary: Progress frames were streamed after every stage; the final result closes the stream. Progress messages are localised in six languages.
nodes.why: A ten-minute request with no feedback is a support ticket. Streaming progress is the interface, not an afterthought.
nodes.guards: Queue heartbeats keep the stream alive through proxies; cancellation propagates back through every stage above.
